items.title: Trump Administration Said to Plan Rolling Back Pregnancy-Related Job Protections
items.summary: The Biden era law was meant to help women stay in the workplace, but some conservatives say rules to enact it went too far with coverage for abortion and fertility treatment.
items.full_text: The Trump administration is preparing to scale back workplace accommodations for women related to pregnancy and reproductive health, seven people with knowledge of discussions of the plans said. The moves will limit the impact of a 2022 law that was meant to fill a gap in disability and discrimination protections that employees are guaranteed at workplaces. It was intended to provide accommodations for pregnant workers, such as bathroom and water breaks, reprieves from heavy lifting or time off for prenatal appointments. But the scope of the regulations under the law, known as the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, has been debated since their drafting. Conservatives, even some who supported the law, said the rule that the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission wrote to apply the law reached far beyond pregnancy to cover matters including abortion, fertility treatment and related procedures and conditions it was not meant to protect. Narrowing them would fit with other efforts by Andrea Lucas , the E.E.O.C.’s chair, to roll back what she has called the liberal excesses of the Biden administration. The E.E.O.C. has targeted corporate diversity, equity and inclusion programs, abandoned some discrimination cases and stopped enforcing workplace protections for transgender workers. It is of a piece with a suite of executive actions that are remaking the American workplace by halting enforcement of sexual harassment rules and encouraging fewer mothers to work outside the home. The E.E.O.C. plans to publish the proposed narrowing of conditions eligible for accommodations as soon as this month.

items.title: William Nordhaus Pioneered Putting a Price on Pollution
items.summary: Economist William Nordhaus said putting a price on pollution was the best way to reduce climate change. Then came the fossil fuel lobby and the anti-tax movement.
items.full_text: Long before climate change entered the vernacular, the economist William D. Nordhaus had seized on the idea of taxing pollution as the most effective way to combat man-made global warming. Dr. Nordhaus, who died Friday at 85, spent his career championing the idea of a tax on carbon dioxide. Putting a price on planet-warming pollution, he contended, would slow down climate change and could be achieved without severe harm to the economy. His work helped inform government policies around the world, and in 2018 he shared the Nobel Prize in economics. But Dr. Nordhaus faced powerful adversaries who ultimately curtailed the influence of his ideas. The fossil fuel industry, which would have absorbed the costs that Dr. Nordhaus proposed, vigorously opposed his work and commissioned reports that attacked carbon taxes. “What economists did not take account for a long time was the enormous political interests that were lined up to fight any kind of climate policy,” said Gilbert E. Metcalf, emeritus professor of economics at Tufts University. “Basically, the fossil fuel industry had a lot of money and they spent it wisely to block any progress in this area.”
